ohms_law_inverse_confusion.summary: Believes current rises when resistance rises at constant voltage.
ohms_law_inverse_confusion.correct_model: At constant voltage, current is inversely proportional to resistance. I = V/R, so if R doubles, I halves. Resistance opposes flow.
ohms_law_inverse_confusion.analogy: A wider pipe lets more water through for the same pump pressure. Narrowing the pipe adds resistance, so less water flows, not more.
ohms_law_inverse_confusion.diagnostic: A 12 V battery drives a 4 ohm resistor. If you swap it for an 8 ohm resistor, does the current go up, go down, or stay the same? Give the number.

voltage_current_conflation.summary: Treats voltage and current as the same quantity.
voltage_current_conflation.correct_model: Voltage is the work done per unit charge between two points. Current is the rate at which charge flows. Voltage causes current; they are different quantities with different units.
voltage_current_conflation.analogy: Voltage is the pressure difference across a pump. Current is how many litres per second actually move.
voltage_current_conflation.diagnostic: A wire carries 2 A when 6 V is applied. Which quantity would change if you made the wire thicker but kept the battery the same, and why?

resistance_area_direct.summary: Thinks a thicker wire has more resistance.
resistance_area_direct.correct_model: Resistance is inversely proportional to cross-sectional area. R = rho*l/A, so doubling the area halves the resistance.
resistance_area_direct.analogy: A wide doorway lets a crowd out faster than a narrow one. More width means less obstruction, not more.
resistance_area_direct.diagnostic: Two copper wires have the same length, but one is twice as thick. Which has the lower resistance, and by what factor?

resistance_length_inverse.summary: Thinks a longer wire has less resistance.
resistance_length_inverse.correct_model: Resistance is directly proportional to length. R = rho*l/A, so a wire twice as long has twice the resistance.
resistance_length_inverse.analogy: Walking down a long crowded corridor takes more effort than a short one. More corridor means more obstruction.
resistance_length_inverse.diagnostic: You cut a 10 ohm wire exactly in half. What is the resistance of one piece?

series_current_divides.summary: Thinks current splits between resistors in series.
series_current_divides.correct_model: In series there is only one path, so the same current flows through every component. It is the voltage that divides.
series_current_divides.analogy: A single-file queue through several doorways: everyone passes through every doorway, so the rate is the same at each.
series_current_divides.diagnostic: Three resistors in series carry 0.5 A through the first. What current flows through the third, and what does divide between them instead?

parallel_resistance_adds.summary: Adds resistances directly when they are in parallel.
parallel_resistance_adds.correct_model: In parallel the reciprocals add: 1/R = 1/R1 + 1/R2. The combined resistance is always LESS than the smallest individual resistor.
parallel_resistance_adds.analogy: Opening a second checkout lane cannot make the queue slower. More paths means less total obstruction.
parallel_resistance_adds.diagnostic: Two 10 ohm resistors are connected in parallel. Is the total more or less than 10 ohms, and what is it exactly?

power_equals_current.summary: Treats power and current as interchangeable.
power_equals_current.correct_model: Power is the rate of energy transfer, P = VI. Current alone does not fix the power, because the voltage matters too.
power_equals_current.analogy: Current is how many coins per second pass you. Power also depends on how valuable each coin is.
power_equals_current.diagnostic: Two devices both draw 2 A, one at 12 V and one at 240 V. Do they consume the same power? Show the numbers.

heating_independent_of_resistance.summary: Thinks heat produced does not depend on resistance.
heating_independent_of_resistance.correct_model: Joule's law: H = I^2*R*t. Heat is directly proportional to resistance for a given current, which is why a heating element is deliberately high-resistance.
heating_independent_of_resistance.analogy: Rubbing your hands together harder, against more friction, makes more heat. Resistance is the electrical friction.
heating_independent_of_resistance.diagnostic: Why is the heating coil in a toaster made of nichrome rather than copper, when both carry the same current?

heavier_falls_faster.summary: Believes heavier objects fall faster in the absence of air resistance.
heavier_falls_faster.correct_model: In a vacuum all objects accelerate at the same g regardless of mass. Greater mass means greater force but also greater inertia, and they cancel.
heavier_falls_faster.analogy: A feather and a hammer dropped on the Moon land together, because there is no air to slow the feather.
heavier_falls_faster.diagnostic: A 1 kg and a 10 kg ball are dropped together in a vacuum from 20 m. Which lands first, and why?

force_needed_for_motion.summary: Thinks continuous force is required to keep something moving.
force_needed_for_motion.correct_model: An object in motion stays in motion unless a net external force acts. Force is needed to CHANGE motion, not to sustain it.
force_needed_for_motion.analogy: A puck slides across smooth ice with nothing pushing it. It slows only because of friction, not because it "runs out" of motion.
force_needed_for_motion.diagnostic: A spacecraft switches off its engines far from any planet. Does it slow down, speed up, or continue at constant velocity?

action_reaction_cancel.summary: Thinks action and reaction cancel so nothing can accelerate.
action_reaction_cancel.correct_model: Action and reaction act on DIFFERENT bodies, so they never cancel on the same body. Only forces on the same object can cancel.
action_reaction_cancel.analogy: When you push off a wall on a skateboard, the wall pushes you. The two forces act on different things, so you move.
action_reaction_cancel.diagnostic: A horse pulls a cart. If the cart pulls back equally, how does the pair ever move forward?

mass_weight_confusion.correct_model: Mass is the amount of matter, in kilograms, and does not change with location. Weight is the force of gravity on that mass, in newtons.
mass_weight_confusion.analogy: Your mass on the Moon is unchanged, but you weigh about a sixth as much, because the Moon pulls more weakly.
mass_weight_confusion.diagnostic: An astronaut has a mass of 70 kg on Earth. What is her mass on the Moon, and what is her weight there?

fraction_addition_denominators.correct_model: Fractions must share a denominator before adding. 1/2 + 1/3 becomes 3/6 + 2/6 = 5/6.
fraction_addition_denominators.analogy: Half a pizza plus a third of a pizza is more than half a pizza. 2/5 is less than half, so it cannot be right.
fraction_addition_denominators.diagnostic: What is 1/4 + 1/4? Now check your method against that answer.

negative_squared_negative.summary: Thinks squaring a negative number gives a negative result.
negative_squared_negative.correct_model: A negative times a negative is positive, so (-3)^2 = 9. Only -3^2 without brackets means -(3^2) = -9.
negative_squared_negative.analogy: Two reversals return you to the original direction: turning around twice leaves you facing forward.
negative_squared_negative.diagnostic: Evaluate (-4)^2 and -4^2 separately, and explain why they differ.

correlation_implies_causation.correct_model: Correlation shows two variables move together. It cannot by itself establish that one causes the other; a third factor may drive both.
correlation_implies_causation.analogy: Ice cream sales and drowning rise together. Neither causes the other; hot weather drives both.
correlation_implies_causation.diagnostic: Shoe size correlates with reading ability in children. Does bigger footwear cause better reading? What explains it?

percentage_change_symmetry.summary: Thinks a 50 percent fall is undone by a 50 percent rise.
percentage_change_symmetry.correct_model: Percentages apply to the current value. 100 falls by 50 percent to 50; a 50 percent rise on 50 returns only 75.
percentage_change_symmetry.analogy: Losing half your money then gaining half of what remains leaves you poorer than you started.
percentage_change_symmetry.diagnostic: A share falls 20 percent then rises 20 percent. Is it back to its original price? Work it out from 100.

division_always_shrinks.summary: Believes dividing always produces a smaller number.
division_always_shrinks.correct_model: Dividing by a number less than 1 increases the value. 6 divided by 0.5 is 12, because 0.5 fits into 6 twelve times.
division_always_shrinks.analogy: How many half-slices fit in six slices? Twelve. Cutting into smaller pieces gives you more pieces.
division_always_shrinks.diagnostic: Compute 10 divided by 0.25 and explain why the answer is larger than 10.

plants_only_photosynthesise.summary: Thinks plants photosynthesise but do not respire.
plants_only_photosynthesise.correct_model: Plants respire continuously, day and night. In daylight photosynthesis simply exceeds respiration, so there is net oxygen release.
plants_only_photosynthesise.analogy: A factory that both makes and consumes electricity still consumes it at night, when production stops.
plants_only_photosynthesise.diagnostic: Does a plant in a sealed dark box consume oxygen? Explain what happens over a whole day and night.

evolution_is_individual.summary: Thinks individual organisms evolve during their lifetime.
evolution_is_individual.correct_model: Populations evolve, not individuals. Heritable variation plus differential survival changes allele frequencies across generations.
evolution_is_individual.analogy: A single brick does not change shape. The wall's overall pattern changes as different bricks are chosen over many rebuilds.
evolution_is_individual.diagnostic: If a weightlifter builds muscle, will their children be born stronger? What does that tell you about how evolution works?

dna_and_gene_same.summary: Uses DNA, gene and chromosome interchangeably.
dna_and_gene_same.correct_model: DNA is the molecule. A gene is a stretch of DNA coding for a product. A chromosome is a packaged length of DNA containing many genes.
dna_and_gene_same.analogy: DNA is the text, a gene is one instruction in it, a chromosome is a whole volume on the shelf.
dna_and_gene_same.diagnostic: Put DNA, gene and chromosome in order from smallest to largest and say why.

immunity_from_antibiotics.correct_model: Antibiotics target bacterial structures and processes. Viruses lack those structures, so antibiotics have no effect on viral infections.
immunity_from_antibiotics.analogy: A key cut for one lock will not open a completely different mechanism.
immunity_from_antibiotics.diagnostic: You have a common cold caused by a virus. Will antibiotics shorten it? What harm might taking them do?

mass_lost_in_burning.summary: Thinks mass disappears when something burns.
mass_lost_in_burning.correct_model: Mass is conserved. The products include gases that escape, so the residue weighs less while the total mass of everything is unchanged.
mass_lost_in_burning.analogy: Money moved from your wallet to your bank account has not vanished; it is simply somewhere you are not counting.
mass_lost_in_burning.diagnostic: Wood burns and the ash weighs far less. Where did the missing mass go, and how would you weigh it?

atoms_change_in_reaction.summary: Thinks atoms are created or destroyed during a reaction.
atoms_change_in_reaction.correct_model: Atoms are rearranged, not created or destroyed. This is why chemical equations must balance on both sides.
atoms_change_in_reaction.analogy: Rebuilding a Lego house into a Lego car uses exactly the same bricks in a different arrangement.
atoms_change_in_reaction.diagnostic: Why must the number of each type of atom be the same on both sides of a balanced equation?

strong_acid_means_concentrated.correct_model: Strength describes how completely an acid dissociates. Concentration describes how much acid is dissolved. A dilute strong acid exists.
strong_acid_means_concentrated.analogy: Strength is how loud each person can shout; concentration is how many people are in the room.
strong_acid_means_concentrated.diagnostic: Is a very dilute solution of hydrochloric acid a strong acid or a weak one? Explain the difference you are using.

bonds_release_energy.correct_model: Breaking bonds absorbs energy; forming bonds releases it. A reaction is exothermic when the bonds formed are stronger than those broken.
bonds_release_energy.analogy: Pulling two magnets apart takes effort; letting them snap together gives that energy back.
bonds_release_energy.diagnostic: In combustion, energy is released overall. Does that mean bond breaking or bond making dominates? Which absorbs energy?

assignment_is_equality.summary: Reads `=` as a mathematical equality rather than assignment.
assignment_is_equality.correct_model: `=` stores the value on the right into the name on the left. `x = x + 1` reads the old value, adds one, and stores the result back.
assignment_is_equality.analogy: A whiteboard: you read the number, add one, wipe it, write the new number.
assignment_is_equality.diagnostic: After `x = 5` then `x = x + 3`, what is x, and what happened in what order?

mutable_default_argument.summary: Expects a mutable default argument to reset on each call.
mutable_default_argument.correct_model: Default arguments are evaluated once, when the function is defined. A mutable default is shared across every call. Use None and create inside.
mutable_default_argument.analogy: One shared shopping basket left by the door, not a fresh basket per trip.
mutable_default_argument.diagnostic: What does calling `f()` three times print, if `def f(a=[]): a.append(1); print(a)`? Why?

reference_vs_copy.summary: Thinks assigning a list creates an independent copy.
reference_vs_copy.correct_model: Assignment binds another name to the same object. Mutating through one name is visible through the other. Copy explicitly with list(a) or a.copy().
reference_vs_copy.analogy: Two people with the address of the same house. Repainting it changes what both of them see.
reference_vs_copy.diagnostic: After `a = [1,2]; b = a; b.append(3)`, what is `a`, and why?

loop_variable_scope.summary: Expects a loop variable to vanish after the loop in Python.
loop_variable_scope.correct_model: Python loops do not create a new scope. The loop variable persists after the loop with its final value.
loop_variable_scope.analogy: The counter on a turnstile still shows its last reading after everyone has gone through.
loop_variable_scope.diagnostic: After `for i in range(3): pass`, what is the value of `i`?

recursion_no_base_case.summary: Writes recursion without recognising the need for a base case.
recursion_no_base_case.correct_model: Every recursive function needs a base case that returns without recursing, or it recurses until the stack is exhausted.
recursion_no_base_case.analogy: Two mirrors facing each other reflect forever because nothing ever stops the process.
recursion_no_base_case.diagnostic: What happens when you call a factorial function that never checks for n equal to 0 or 1?

float_equality.summary: Expects exact equality when comparing floating point results.
float_equality.correct_model: Binary floating point cannot represent 0.1 exactly, so sums carry tiny errors. Compare with a tolerance, or use decimal for money.
float_equality.analogy: Writing one third as 0.333 in a fixed number of digits: three of them do not add back to exactly 1.
float_equality.diagnostic: Does `0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3` evaluate to True in Python? What should you write instead?

off_by_one_range.correct_model: `range(n)` yields 0 to n-1, n values in total. The upper bound is exclusive.
off_by_one_range.analogy: A fence with 5 posts has 4 gaps between them. Counting boundaries and counting items give different totals.
off_by_one_range.diagnostic: How many numbers does `range(5)` produce, and what is the largest?
